solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.protects: CABLE wraps round the single letter, keeping it safe inside

blocks.note: a guy is a rope or cable steadying a mast or tent

annotation.surface: Someone praised as friendly because a bloke looks after a lone person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guy' reads as a man looking after someone; the setter means a guy rope, the line that holds a tent upright.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sociable person seeks out company and is friendly towards others.

indicatorNotes.detailed: read as de-tailed: AND loses its tail letter

blocks.note: with = AND, minus its last letter

annotation.surface: A political party's carefully worked-out motto, with Labour as the British party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'elaborate', but split it as de-tailed: a word losing its tail. Labour is also a British political party, which suits the motto picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a slogan is a short memorable phrase adopted by a party or firm, which is what a motto is.

entries.clue: Covered in blubber, that woman’s red (6)

indicatorNotes.Covered in: HER sits inside CRY, covered by it

blocks.note: to blubber is to cry noisily

annotation.surface: A woman smeared with whale fat has gone red in the face.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blubber' pretends to be whale fat but is the verb, to weep. The ’s stands for 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Defined by shade: cherry names the bright red of the fruit, so it is one kind of red.

entries.clue: Active US soldier with bitter exterior? (5)

indicatorNotes.with: joins the soldier to the beer that goes round him
indicatorNotes.exterior: ALE forms the outside, with GI in the middle

blocks.note: bitter is a British style of ale

annotation.surface: A lively American soldier who seems sour on the outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' reads as an adjective about the soldier's manner, but it is a noun: bitter is a hoppy British beer.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: someone agile moves quickly and nimbly, which is being physically active.

indicatorNotes.not: the letters for 'namely' are taken out

annotation.surface: An odd remark about underwear and stays, stays being old-fashioned corsets.
annotation.walkthrough: Stays sound like more underwear (corsets), but here the word is the verb: remains.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: whoever lingers stays on longer than expected.

entries.clue: Sins left facing parts of church (6)

indicatorNotes.facing: L stands in front of APSES

blocks.note: apses are the rounded end sections of a church

annotation.surface: Sins committed facing certain areas of a church.
annotation.walkthrough: The church setting makes 'Sins' feel like part of the scene, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A mild synonym: lapses are moral slips or failings, the lesser end of sins.

indicatorNotes.extremely: take only the extremes, first and last letters, of 'accomplished'

blocks.note: first and last letters of accomplished
an oration is a formal speech

annotation.surface: Praise for a wonderfully accomplished speech.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as 'very', but it asks for the extremes of the next word.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym by degree: adoration is intense, worshipful love.

indicatorNotes.almost: the word is not quite complete: last letter off

blocks.note: as in 'this is the king' = this represents the king
end = TERM, missing its last letter

annotation.surface: A wicked fault that nearly spells the end.
annotation.walkthrough: TERM is an end, as in the end of a period or a contract.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sinister means evil or menacing, as wicked does.

blocks.note: like Uriah Heep, the 'ever so 'umble' clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield

annotation.surface: Someone embarrassed, and humble in a dropped-aitch accent.
annotation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield keeps calling himself 'umble', so rather 'umble means like Heep.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: sheepish describes the awkward, embarrassed look of someone ashamed of what they did.

entries.clue: Docile old criminal taking cut out (8)

indicatorNotes.taking: to take something in is to receive it inside, so BENT takes DIE into its middle

blocks.note: bent = crooked, criminal (British slang, as in a bent copper)
an engine that cuts out dies

annotation.surface: An old criminal gone meek after being dealt out of a scheme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut out' sounds like being excluded, but it is what a stalling engine does.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a docile creature is obedient, doing as it is told without fuss.

blocks.note: the ounce is the snow leopard

annotation.surface: A black cat suddenly leaping.
annotation.walkthrough: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a crossword favourite.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: a bounce is a quick springing leap, as of a ball off the ground.

entries.clue: Stop male under stone hugging sweetheart (4)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, M comes below ST
indicatorNotes.hugging: ST and M together clasp the E
indicatorNotes.sweetheart: the heart of 'sweet' is its middle letter

blocks.note: st = stone, the British unit of weight

annotation.surface: A man stretched under a gravestone, clutching his beloved.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' is a lover on the surface, but it means the heart of the word 'sweet'.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to stem bleeding or a tide of complaints is to stop it flowing.

entries.clue: Welcome holding hands after a union (9)

indicatorNotes.holding: to hold is to keep something in your grasp, so GREET keeps MEN within it
indicatorNotes.after: coming after means following in sequence, so the wrapped word follows A

annotation.surface: A welcome for a newly married couple holding hands.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are the workers of farmhand and deckhand, not palms being held.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a union can be a pact or accord between parties, which is an agreement.

indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling the wrong way, so POSE is read from right to left

blocks.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose

annotation.surface: An instruction to lean back after an ace, as if at the card table.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sit' is posing for a painter, not taking a seat.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: Aesop, the ancient Greek author of fables, is a famous storyteller.

indicatorNotes.regularly in: take every other letter within the next word

blocks.note: fArMhOuSe: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

annotation.surface: A character from a farming soap who is always turning up at the farmhouse.
annotation.walkthrough: Emmerdale is a long-running British TV soap set in rural Yorkshire, so the farmhouse fits its world.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Amos Brearly ran the village pub in Emmerdale for decades.

entries.clue: Rabbit to put in bare emporium (9)

indicatorNotes.put in: GAS and TO go inside MERE

blocks.note: to rabbit (on) is British slang for chattering; so is to gas

annotation.surface: Someone putting a rabbit into an empty shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is the animal on the surface, but in British slang to rabbit on is to chatter endlessly.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: a megastore is a very large shop, and an emporium is a grand store.

blocks.note: gIdDiEr: second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: A man hugging girls who now and then get a little dizzy.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s of 'Chap’s' is part of the wordplay, not a link: it supplies the final S.
annotation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned synonym: maidens are girls or young unmarried women.

entries.clue: Sites with power casual about energy (8)

indicatorNotes.about: about in the sense of around, so REMISS stands all round the E
indicatorNotes.with: with means accompanied by, so P simply joins on in front

annotation.surface: Power-station sites run carelessly with respect to energy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' in the surface; in the wordplay it means going round.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym: premises are the buildings and land a business occupies, its sites.

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, the first pieces sit above DATE

blocks.note: a date is an engagement, an appointment

annotation.surface: Swamping a sister with fuss over her engagement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engagement' suggests a betrothal but is simply an appointment.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym by metaphor: to inundate is literally to flood, and figuratively to overwhelm with too much.

entries.clue: Grass keeping info back broke promises (7)

indicatorNotes.keeping: REED keeps the turned letters inside
indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling the wrong way, so GEN is read from right to left

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass
gen is British slang for information

annotation.surface: An informer, a grass, withheld information and went back on his word.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grass' reads as an informer (British slang for one who tells the police), but it is the plant.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to renege is to go back on a promise or deal.

entries.clue: Disregard of French family after vacation (4)

indicatorNotes.after vacation: the word is vacated, emptied of its middle

blocks.note: FamilY emptied, leaving the outside letters

annotation.surface: A French family ignoring things once back from holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vacation' reads as a holiday, but it means emptying: the word is vacated.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: to defy an order is to disregard it openly.

indicatorNotes.soundly: spoken, the word sounds like another

annotation.surface: A coin that was properly minted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast' suggests metal poured into a mould, which fits a coin, but here it means thrown.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the cent, a hundredth of a dollar or euro, is a small coin.

blocks.note: to fly is to hurry, hasten

annotation.surface: Catching a fly makes someone lose their temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temper' looks like anger, but it is the verb: to moderate or restrain.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to chasten someone is to subdue or moderate them, just as to temper is.

entries.clue: Sound of cool band round room (6)

indicatorNotes.Sound of: the answer sounds like the word for 'cool'

annotation.surface: A cool music group playing to the room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' pretends to be a group of musicians; it is a decorated strip running round a wall.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a frieze is the decorated strip running along the top of a room's walls.

annotation.surface: Hiring a yacht to sail round another boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' is a boat in the sailing picture, but here it is a blood vessel.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: arteries carry blood from the heart, one of the body's vessels.

entries.clue: Shocks from electricity supply, we hear (5)

indicatorNotes.we hear: the answer sounds like the phrase before it

blocks.note: the mains is the household electricity supply

annotation.surface: Electric shocks from the power supply.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shocks' in an electrical surface means jolts, but here it is shocks of hair.
annotation.definitionFit: A second-sense synonym: a shock of hair is a thick bushy mass of it, as a mane is.

entries.clue: Sycophant is more prostrate before Queen (9)

blocks.note: prostrate = lying flat, so more prostrate = flatter

annotation.surface: A crawler bows lower still before the Queen.
annotation.walkthrough: The courtier bowing before the Queen is exactly what a sycophant does, so surface and answer match.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sycophant wins favour by excessive praise, which makes one a flatterer.

entries.clue: Times expressed musically, perhaps Italian initially? (5)

blocks.note: reads as times sung or played, perhaps the newspaper set to music; the setter means musical speeds
the terms for speeds in music come from Italian, and this Italian plural ends in the I that 'Italian' begins with

annotation.surface: A question whether musical time markings started out in Italian.
annotation.walkthrough: Tempo markings such as allegro and adagio are Italian, which is why the plural keeps the Italian ending.
annotation.definitionFit: Tempi, the Italian plural of tempo, are the speeds or times at which music is played.

annotation.surface: Big waves in the question of the sea's saltiness.
annotation.walkthrough: The seaside picture makes 'salt' a noun, a sailor or sea water; it is the verb, as in the kitchen.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: salting food is one way to season it, flavouring it before serving.

blocks.note: reads as shares on the market; the setter means livestock such as cattle
reads as a share issue or a problem; the setter means an outpouring, the herd issuing forth all at once

annotation.surface: A surprise share issue on the stock market.
annotation.walkthrough: The financial reading is the trap: stock is a farmer's herd, and the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden panicked rush of cattle or horses, so it is livestock pouring out without warning.

entries.clue: Stick waste pipe around sink, finally (6)

blocks.note: a sewer is a waste pipe

annotation.surface: Plumbing instructions to jam a stick in the drain around the sink.
annotation.walkthrough: The plumbing scene makes 'Stick' sound like a rod, but read it as the verb, to pierce.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to skewer is to stick a spike right through something.

indicatorNotes.about: ELY goes round the other letters

blocks.note: a see is a bishop's diocese; Ely is one, in Cambridgeshire

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether to look into a new car exhaust, answered with an emphatic yes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'See' reads as look, but it is a bishop's see, and Ely, a cathedral city in England, is the crossword's favourite.
annotation.definitionFit: An exclamation synonym: 'Entirely!' and 'Absolutely!' are both emphatic ways to agree completely.
